questions.content:
Question 1: Tectonic hazards

Two earthquakes of similar strength struck coastal regions on destructive plate margins in the same year. The table shows the data.

Earthquake X (Country X, high-income): magnitude 7.2 | focal depth 10 km | people exposed 2.4 million | deaths 18 | injuries 410
Earthquake Y (Country Y, low-income): magnitude 7.1 | focal depth 12 km | people exposed 3.1 million | deaths 6,200 | injuries 21,500

In both countries an oceanic plate is being forced beneath a continental plate.

(a) Calculate the number of deaths per 100,000 people exposed for Earthquake Y. Show your working. (2 marks)
(b) State what an increase of one whole number on the moment magnitude scale means for the size of the ground shaking measured by a seismograph. (1 mark)
(c) Explain how an earthquake is caused at a destructive plate margin like this one. (3 marks)
(d) Explain why Earthquake Y caused far more deaths than Earthquake X, even though the two earthquakes had similar magnitudes. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) Correct working: 6,200 / 3,100,000 x 100,000 (or 6,200 / 31).
[1] (a) Answer 200 deaths per 100,000 people exposed. ECF if exposed population misread but method correct (award the method mark only).
[1] (b) The measured ground shaking (amplitude) is about 10 times larger (accept: roughly 32 times more energy released). Do not accept "twice as big".
[1] (c) Plates move towards each other / the denser oceanic plate subducts beneath the continental plate.
[1] (c) The plates stick because of friction and stress/strain builds up.
[1] (c) The plates suddenly slip when the stress exceeds the friction, releasing energy as seismic waves from the focus.
[1] (d) Credit for the first developed reason: Country Y has weaker, poorly enforced building standards so buildings collapse (point plus development).
[1] (d) Second developed reason: Country Y has fewer emergency services/hospitals, so injured people are not treated and deaths rise.
[1] (d) Third developed reason: more people live in dense informal housing, or there was little earthquake preparedness/warning and education.
[1] (d) A comparative link to Country X, e.g. earthquake-proof buildings, drills and a wealthier recovery capacity limited deaths there.
Common errors: confusing magnitude with intensity; describing damage rather than explaining the cause; saying Country Y had a bigger earthquake (the data show Earthquake X was slightly stronger). Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Question 2: Rivers and fieldwork enquiry

A class investigated the hypothesis: "Pebbles become smaller downstream." They measured the longest axis of 10 pebbles at each of 5 sites along the River Tamsin. Selected results (cm):

Site 2: 14, 9, 11, 8, 12, 10, 7, 13, 9, 11
Site 5: 3, 4, 2, 5, 3, 4, 3, 2, 4, 3

(a) Calculate the mean pebble length at Site 2. (2 marks)
(b) The mean pebble length at Site 5 is 3.3 cm. Calculate the percentage decrease in mean pebble length from Site 2 to Site 5. Give your answer to one decimal place. (2 marks)
(c) Design a method the class could use to collect a reliable sample of pebbles at each site. Refer to how pebbles are selected and how they are measured. (4 marks)
(d) Identify one safety risk when working in a river and explain how it could be managed. (2 marks)
(e) State one reason why the results from this enquiry may not fully prove the hypothesis. (1 mark)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) Sum of lengths = 104 cm (or correct method of adding all ten values and dividing by 10).
[1] (a) Mean = 10.4 cm.
[1] (b) Correct working: (10.4 - 3.3) / 10.4 x 100.
[1] (b) Answer 68.3% (accept 68.27, 68.3). ECF from an incorrect mean in (a).
[1] (c) Random or systematic selection without bias, e.g. walking across the channel and picking the pebble at the toe of each step, or using random numbers to choose grid positions (no picking by eye).
[1] (c) A suitably large sample, e.g. at least 10 pebbles at each site, at the same part of the channel each time.
[1] (c) A clear measurement method, e.g. measure the longest axis with a ruler/calipers in cm, to the nearest millimetre, by the same person.
[1] (c) A reliability improvement, e.g. repeat on another day or find the mean/median, record in a prepared table.
[1] (d) Valid risk, e.g. slipping on rocks, deep or fast water, cold water, or polluted water.
[1] (d) Linked management, e.g. wear appropriate footwear and work in pairs, check depth/flow beforehand, stay in shallow water, use gloves and wash hands.
[1] (e) Valid limitation, e.g. small sample, only one river on one day, bias in picking pebbles, or rock type changes could also explain the pattern.
Common errors: dividing by 11 or 9 in (a); using Site 5 as the base in (b), which gives 215.2% and earns no mark. Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Question 3: Coasts

The cliffs at Hallow Bay are made of soft clay and sand. Surveyors measured the retreat of the cliff edge at four points between 2010 and 2020.

Point P: 12 m | Point Q: 31 m | Point R: 8 m | Point S: 19 m

A house at Point Q is currently 40 m from the cliff edge.

(a) Calculate the mean annual rate of cliff retreat across the four points. (2 marks)
(b) Assuming the rate of retreat at Point Q stays constant, estimate how many years it will be before the cliff edge reaches the house. Give your answer to the nearest year and state one reason why your estimate may be inaccurate. (3 marks)
(c) Explain how a wave-cut platform forms. (4 marks)
(d) Suggest two reasons why the rate of retreat differs between Points P, Q, R and S. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) Total retreat = 70 m over 4 points, mean = 17.5 m over ten years (working).
[1] (a) Answer 1.75 m per year.
[1] (b) Rate at Q = 31 / 10 = 3.1 m per year.
[1] (b) 40 / 3.1 = 12.9, so approximately 13 years.
[1] (b) Valid reason, e.g. storms can cause sudden large falls so the rate is not constant, sea level rise, or coastal defences may be added. ECF on rate from (a) if 1.75 used (40 / 1.75 = 22.9 years, so 23 years) but then only award the working marks.
[1] (c) Waves attack the base of the cliff by hydraulic action and abrasion, forming a wave-cut notch.
[1] (c) The rock above the notch becomes unsupported.
[1] (c) The cliff collapses and retreats inland.
[1] (c) The gently sloping rock surface left behind is the wave-cut platform, exposed at low tide (the process repeats as the cliff retreats).
[1] (d) First valid reason, e.g. rock type/geology, presence of defences, exposure to the prevailing wind and fetch.
[1] (d) Second different valid reason, e.g. beach width protecting the cliff base, human activity or drainage causing slumping.
Common errors: confusing erosion with deposition; saying 'waves wash the cliff away' without a process. Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Question 4: Weather and climate

The table gives the monthly rainfall for the city of Dhanora, which has a tropical monsoon climate.

Rainfall (mm): Jan 8 | Feb 10 | Mar 20 | Apr 45 | May 110 | Jun 260 | Jul 340 | Aug 310 | Sep 190 | Oct 70 | Nov 20 | Dec 9
Mean monthly temperature (degrees Celsius): Jan 24 | Feb 26 | Mar 29 | Apr 32 | May 33 | Jun 30 | Jul 28 | Aug 28 | Sep 28 | Oct 28 | Nov 26 | Dec 24

(a) Calculate the annual rainfall total. (1 mark)
(b) State the annual temperature range. (1 mark)
(c) Calculate the percentage of the annual rainfall that falls between June and September inclusive. Give your answer to the nearest whole number. (2 marks)
(d) Describe the seasonal pattern of rainfall in Dhanora. Use data from the table. (2 marks)
(e) Explain why Dhanora has a wet season and a dry season. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) 1,392 mm.
[1] (b) 33 - 24 = 9 degrees Celsius.
[1] (c) Correct working: (260 + 340 + 310 + 190) = 1,100, then 1,100 / 1,392 x 100.
[1] (c) Answer 79%. ECF from an incorrect total in (a).
[1] (d) Identifies the wet season, June to September (peak in July at 340 mm), and the dry season, November to March, with a data quote.
[1] (d) A contrast with data, e.g. July has about 42 times as much rain as January (340 / 8), or a gradual build-up from April.
[1] (e) In summer the land heats faster than the sea, creating low pressure over land (the ITCZ moves north).
[1] (e) Moist south-westerly winds blow from the ocean to the land, bringing humid air.
[1] (e) The air rises, cools and condenses to give heavy convectional/relief rainfall (wet season).
[1] (e) In winter the wind direction reverses, so dry air blows from the land, giving the dry season.
Common errors: stating that it is 'hot so rains'; missing wind direction; giving the range as 24-33 without calculating. Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Question 5: Ecosystems

The Okavi tropical rainforest is a biodiversity hotspot. Ecologists estimate that its nutrients are stored as follows: biomass 74 percent, litter 2 percent, soil 24 percent. Part of the forest has been converted to farmland over the last thirty years. Forest cover data:

1990: 8.4 million hectares
2020: 5.9 million hectares

(a) State which store holds the most nutrients in the Okavi forest. (1 mark)
(b) Explain why the soils of tropical rainforests are often infertile even though the vegetation is lush. (3 marks)
(c) Calculate the percentage loss of forest cover between 1990 and 2020 (to one decimal place), and the mean area lost per year in hectares. (3 marks)
(d) Explain two ways in which deforestation can damage the ecosystem. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) Biomass (74 percent).
[1] (b) Rapid decomposition in the hot, wet conditions means litter is broken down quickly.
[1] (b) Nutrients are taken up immediately by plant roots and stored in the biomass, so little stays in the soil.
[1] (b) Heavy rainfall leaches remaining nutrients out of the soil (accept: thin litter layer).
[1] (c) Loss = 8.4 - 5.9 = 2.5 million hectares; percentage = 2.5 / 8.4 x 100 = 29.8%.
[1] (c) Mean loss per year = 2,500,000 / 30 = about 83,333 hectares per year (accept 83,000).
[1] (c) Correct units and one decimal place given. ECF applies to an arithmetic slip in the loss.
[1] (d) First impact identified, e.g. loss of habitat leading to loss of biodiversity or extinction.
[1] (d) Development of first impact, e.g. species are specialised and cannot adapt, food webs collapse.
[1] (d) Second impact identified, e.g. soil erosion and nutrient loss after tree removal, or reduced carbon storage and more CO2.
[1] (d) Development of second impact, e.g. no roots to bind soil so heavy rain washes soil into rivers causing flooding/silting.
Common errors: giving percentage of 2.5 / 5.9 = 42.4% (wrong base); omitting units; describing causes rather than impacts. Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Question 6: Urbanisation

Dalmora is a rapidly urbanising country. In 2020 its population was 24 million. The proportion of people living in cities has risen from 31 percent in 1990 to 56 percent in 2020. Most growth is in the capital, where around a third of residents live in informal settlements built on steep land with no sewers.

(a) Calculate the number of people living in cities in Dalmora in 2020. (2 marks)
(b) Describe how the urban population has changed between 1990 and 2020. (2 marks)
(c) Explain why Dalmora's cities are growing so rapidly. (3 marks)
(d) Discuss one strategy that could improve living conditions in the informal settlements. Refer to a benefit and a limitation. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) Correct working: 56 / 100 x 24 million.
[1] (a) Answer 13.44 million (13,440,000).
[1] (b) Urban population share increased from 31 percent to 56 percent, a rise of 25 percentage points.
[1] (b) Further description: more than half of the population is now urban, or the share nearly doubled (1.8 times).
[1] (c) Rural-urban migration is caused by push factors (e.g. poverty, land shortage) and pull factors (e.g. jobs, services).
[1] (c) Migrants are often young adults so there is a high birth rate (natural increase) in the cities.
[1] (c) Development of one point, e.g. cities offer higher wages and better schools and hospitals.
[1] (d) Identifies a suitable strategy (e.g. self-help scheme, providing piped water and sanitation, upgrading housing, community land titles).
[1] (d) A developed benefit, e.g. improves health or reduces disease, communities feel secure when they have titles.
[1] (d) A developed limitation, e.g. costs, slow progress or land on steep slopes is unsafe to develop.
[1] (d) A balanced judgement or conclusion on the strategy.
Common errors: giving 13.44 as thousands; calculating 31 percent of 24 million (7.44 million); confusing urbanisation with urban sprawl. Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Question 7: Population and development

The table compares two countries.

Verdia (low-income): GNI per capita US$2,400 | life expectancy 62 years | population aged 0-14: 38% | aged 15-64: 58% | aged 65 and over: 4%
Nordal (high-income): GNI per capita US$48,000 | life expectancy 83 years | population aged 0-14: 16% | aged 15-64: 63% | aged 65 and over: 21%

The dependency ratio is the number of dependants (under 15 and 65 and over) for every 100 people of working age (15-64).

(a) Calculate how many times greater Nordal's GNI per capita is than Verdia's. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the dependency ratio for each country, giving your answers to the nearest whole number. (3 marks)
(c) Compare the population structures of Verdia and Nordal. (3 marks)
(d) Explain how a high youth dependency ratio can slow development. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) 48,000 / 2,400 = 20 times.
[1] (b) Verdia: (38 + 4) / 58 x 100 = working shown.
[1] (b) Verdia = 72 (accept 72.4).
[1] (b) Nordal: (16 + 21) / 63 x 100 = 59 (accept 58.7).
[1] (c) A similarity or difference in the youth group: Verdia has a much larger share aged 0-14 (38 vs 16).
[1] (c) A contrasting statement on the elderly group: Nordal has far more people aged 65 and over (21 vs 4).
[1] (c) A comparative conclusion, e.g. Verdia has a young, growing population while Nordal has an ageing one; the working-age share is similar.
[1] (d) A large share of children needs spending on schools and healthcare.
[1] (d) Few workers support many dependants, so savings and tax revenue are low.
[1] (d) Development link: less money is available for investment in infrastructure and industry, which keeps incomes low (accept a high birth rate that strains food and housing).
Common errors: using only under-15s as dependants; dividing by the total population; saying Verdia is 'less developed because it has more children' without explanation. Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Question 8: Resources and energy

Kestrel Isle is a remote island that generates 1,200 GWh of electricity each year: diesel 720 GWh, wind 300 GWh, solar 120 GWh, hydro 60 GWh. The government proposes a new wind farm of 12 turbines, each with a capacity of 3 MW. Turbines are expected to produce at 35 percent of their capacity over a year (capacity factor). There are 8,760 hours in a year. Burning diesel emits 0.75 tonnes of CO2 per MWh.

(a) Calculate the percentage of Kestrel Isle's electricity that is renewable. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the expected annual output of the new wind farm in MWh. (3 marks)
(c) Assuming all of its output replaces diesel generation, calculate the CO2 saved each year. Give your answer to the nearest 100 tonnes. (2 marks)
(d) Explain two problems that may reduce the benefits of wind power on the island. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) Renewables = 300 + 120 + 60 = 480 GWh.
[1] (a) 480 / 1,200 x 100 = 40%.
[1] (b) Total capacity = 12 x 3 = 36 MW.
[1] (b) 36 x 0.35 x 8,760 (working).
[1] (b) Answer 110,376 MWh (accept 110,000 or 110 GWh).
[1] (c) 110,376 x 0.75 (ECF from (b)).
[1] (c) Answer approx 82,800 tonnes of CO2 per year.
[1] (d) First developed problem, e.g. wind is intermittent, so diesel backup is still needed when winds are low.
[1] (d) Second developed problem, e.g. turbines harm birds or scenery, which may reduce tourism, or high costs of installing and maintaining turbines on a remote island.
[1] (d) Further development or consequence of either problem, e.g. storage batteries are needed which add cost.
Common errors: forgetting to convert GWh to MWh (1 GWh = 1,000 MWh); using 3 MW as total capacity; not applying the capacity factor. Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Question 9: Managing coasts sustainably

Hallow Bay's council must choose how to manage 2 km of eroding coast. The cliff top has 150 homes worth a combined US$30 million. The options are shown below.

Option A: Concrete sea wall. Cost US$18 million. Lifespan 50 years. Maintenance US$0.2 million per year. Reflects wave energy, which lowers the beach in front of it.
Option B: Rock armour (large boulders). Cost US$9 million. Lifespan 30 years. Maintenance US$0.1 million per year. Looks natural, but boulders are hard to walk over.
Option C: Managed retreat with compensation. Cost US$6 million. Lifespan: permanent. No maintenance. 40 homes are moved back, the rest remain at risk. Creates salt marsh, which absorbs wave energy and provides a habitat.

(a) Calculate the construction cost per metre of coast for Option A. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the construction cost per year of lifespan for Option A and Option B. (2 marks)
(c) State two ways in which hard engineering such as a sea wall can harm the environment. (2 marks)
(d) Evaluate which option is the most sustainable for Hallow Bay. In your answer, consider economic, social and environmental factors and reach a justified conclusion. (8 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) 18,000,000 / 2,000 = US$9,000 per metre.
[1] (b) Option A: 18 / 50 = US$0.36 million per year.
[1] (b) Option B: 9 / 30 = US$0.30 million per year. ECF if (a) values are used consistently.
[1] (c) First valid impact, e.g. waves reflected off the wall scour the beach, reducing it.
[1] (c) Second impact, e.g. loss of natural habitat or the interruption of longshore drift, causing erosion elsewhere.
[1] (d) Economic point with data, e.g. B is cheaper per year (0.30 vs 0.36 million) but needs repeated rebuilding; C is cheapest overall at 6 million with no maintenance.
[1] (d) Economic evaluation, e.g. A protects all 30 million of property and C protects only some, so lost property value must be weighed against costs.
[1] (d) Social point, e.g. residents forced to move under C may resist while A and B keep communities together.
[1] (d) Social evaluation, e.g. fair compensation and consultation might reduce opposition.
[1] (d) Environmental point, e.g. C creates salt marsh and habitat, while A damages the beach.
[1] (d) Environmental evaluation, e.g. rock armour (B) is less harmful than a wall but still alters the natural coast.
[1] (d) Sustainability concept used, e.g. meeting present needs without compromising the future (long-term lifespan, sea level rise, climate change).
[1] (d) A justified conclusion naming one option (or a combination) and a reason with a stated condition or limitation. Any consistent argument can earn full credit; Option C is expected to be argued as most sustainable but do not penalise a well-supported alternative.
Common errors: description of each option without evaluation; ignoring the data; unsupported opinion. Accept other valid points.

questions.content:
Question 10: Globalisation (extended answer)

Tavira is a middle-income country in South-East Asia. Since 2005 a transnational corporation (TNC), Nordwear, has built five clothing factories there.

Tavira's garment exports: 2005 US$2.1 billion | 2020 US$9.8 billion
Factory workers: about 800,000, of whom 80 percent are women. Typical pay is about four times the average farm wage but long working hours are common.
Nordwear's supply chain: cotton from India, fabric milled in China, final assembly in Tavira, sold in Europe and North America.
Environmental concerns: untreated dye water has polluted two rivers. Safety concerns: a factory fire in 2018 killed 41 workers.

(a) Calculate the percentage increase in Tavira's garment exports between 2005 and 2020. Give your answer to one decimal place. (2 marks)
(b) State two factors that have made globalisation of production possible. (2 marks)
(c) To what extent has globalisation benefited the people of Tavira? Use the evidence above and your own knowledge of globalisation. Structure your answer clearly, include a judgement and justify it. (12 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] (a) Correct working: (9.8 - 2.1) / 2.1 x 100.
[1] (a) Answer 366.7% (accept 367%).
[1] (b) First factor, e.g. container shipping and cheaper transport.
[1] (b) Second factor, e.g. the internet and ICT, trade agreements, or falling trade barriers.
[1] (c) Benefit 1 identified from the evidence: employment of 800,000 workers, with pay about four times farm wages.
[1] (c) Benefit 1 developed: rising household incomes can reduce poverty and improve diet, education and health.
[1] (c) Benefit 2: export growth (US$9.8 billion) brings foreign currency and tax revenue.
[1] (c) Benefit 2 developed: government can invest in infrastructure, and the multiplier effect creates jobs in services and transport.
[1] (c) Benefit 3 or women's empowerment: 80 percent of workers are women, so incomes and independence may rise.
[1] (c) Cost 1 identified: poor safety, e.g. 2018 fire killing 41 workers, long hours.
[1] (c) Cost 1 developed: weak regulation, so workers have few rights, and profits flow mostly to the TNC.
[1] (c) Cost 2: environmental damage, e.g. dye pollution of rivers.
[1] (c) Cost 2 developed: pollution harms fishing, drinking water and health, so local people bear the cost.
[1] (c) Wider context: dependence on one industry or on Nordwear's decisions, risk of jobs moving to a cheaper country; or global inequality.
[1] (c) A clear judgement on 'to what extent' that weighs benefits against costs, e.g. 'benefited to a moderate extent'.
[1] (c) The judgement is justified, with a stated condition for more benefit (e.g. stronger regulation, fair wages, enforcement of pollution laws) and consideration of different groups (workers, farmers, the government, the TNC).
Marker note: credit up to 12 marks for these points. A response with only benefits or only costs, or with no judgement, is capped at 7 marks. Responses with a balanced, supported and explicit judgement can reach full marks. Common errors: listing facts without linking them to 'benefit'; no use of the data; ignoring 'to what extent'. Accept other valid points.
